title: Vast Star-Forming Region 30 Doradus
caption: The 30 Doradus Nebula and star cluster R136, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: 30 Doradus, R136 · constellation Dorado · about 170,000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, N. Walborn and J. Maíz-Apellániz (Space Telescope Science Institute, Baltimore, MD), R. Barbá (La Plata Observatory, La Plata, Argentina)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A vast, sculpted landscape of gas and dust surrounds a large blue blob just left of center, the star cluster R136. Around it lies the 30 Doradus Nebula, a star-forming region 170,000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small companion of the Milky Way. The mosaic covers the whole inner nebula, 200 by 150 light-years.

R136 holds several dozen of the heaviest stars known, each roughly 100 solar masses and some 10 times hotter than the Sun, all born together about 2 million years ago. Their ultraviolet light makes the gas glow, and their winds push it away and compress the inner faces of nearby clouds. That pressure is triggering a new generation of stars about 30 to 50 light-years from the cluster, most still hidden in dusty cocoons.

Several finger-like pillars, each several light-years long, point toward R136. Dense clumps shield the material behind them, and stars grow inside. In one spot a trio of stars only a few hundred thousand years old has just broken out of its pillar.

understand.summary: A mosaic of five overlapping pictures from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. NASA describes the colors by feature, with blue for hot stars, green for gas energized by the cluster, pink for cloud edges facing the cluster and reddish-brown for cooler cloud surfaces.
understand.eye: The colors were chosen to bring out features in the stars and nebula, and the mosaic stitches together observations spread over several years.

behind.people: See full credit: NASA, N. Walborn and J. Maíz-Apellániz (Space Telescope Science Institute, Baltimore, MD), R. Barbá (La Plata Observatory, La Plata, Argentina)
behind.exposure: Observation dates per NASA: January 1994 - September 2000.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Hubble's infrared camera, NICMOS, has already found newborn stars inside most of these pillars by seeing through the dust. The pillars match those of the Eagle Nebula in size and would be invisible without Hubble's resolution. In another 2 million years the new stars will be in full bloom, while R136's massive stars will have burned out, leaving a giant empty shell at the center.
sources: NASA release: Hubble’s Panoramic Portrait of a Vast Star-Forming Region
alt: A large blue star cluster left of center, surrounded by greenish and pink glowing gas and reddish-brown clouds with small finger-like pillars.
